summary: Satranidazole is a 5-nitroimidazole antiprotozoal and antimicrobial agent marketed in India (e.g., Satrogyl) for intestinal and hepatic amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, and anaerobic infections. Compared with older nitroimidazoles such as metronidazole, it is reported to have a shorter plasma half-life, fewer gastrointestinal complaints, and a lower likelihood of neurological or disulfiram-like reactions, although the class precaution against concurrent alcohol still applies. It is not FDA-approved.

Anaerobic bacterial infections (per regional prescribing information)

moa: Satranidazole is a 5-nitroimidazole. After passive diffusion into susceptible anaerobic protozoa and bacteria, its nitro group is reduced by microbial electron transport proteins, generating reactive nitro radical intermediates that bind to and disrupt microbial DNA, causing strand breakage and loss of helical structure. This is selectively cytotoxic to anaerobic organisms because the reduction occurs only in the low-redox-potential environment of anaerobes and microaerophiles.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to satranidazole or other nitroimidazoles
relative: Pre-existing neurologic disorders (risk increases with high dose or prolonged use)
monitor: Neurologic symptoms with prolonged or high-dose therapy

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established. As a nitroimidazole, use is generally avoided unless the benefit clearly outweighs the potential risk, and caution is advised particularly during the first trimester. Consult product information and a specialist before use in pregnancy.
lact: Nitroimidazoles are known to distribute into breast milk. Avoid use during breastfeeding, or interrupt nursing during therapy, unless the benefit to the mother clearly outweighs the potential risk to the infant.
renal: Specific renal dose adjustment recommendations are not well established for satranidazole. Use with caution in renal impairment and follow regional prescribing information.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment. Because nitroimidazoles undergo hepatic metabolism, dose reduction may be appropriate in patients with significant liver disease; consult product information.

major: Alcohol and alcohol-containing products (disulfiram-like reaction: flushing, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache)
Disulfiram (risk of acute psychosis/confusion with nitroimidazoles)
moderate: Oral anticoagulants such as warfarin (nitroimidazoles may potentiate anticoagulant effect)
minor: Hepatic enzyme inducers may alter nitroimidazole metabolism
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least 3 days after the last dose due to potential disulfiram-like reaction characteristic of the nitroimidazole class (satranidazole is reported to have a lower incidence than older agents, but avoidance is still advised)
interactions.diagnostics: No specific assay interference well established; data not established

serious: Peripheral neuropathy with prolonged or high-dose use
rare: Central nervous system effects (confusion, seizures) with excessive dosing
emergency: Severe hypersensitivity / anaphylaxis (difficulty breathing, swelling, widespread rash) - seek emergency care
Disulfiram-like reaction after alcohol (severe flushing, vomiting, palpitations)

pearls: Not FDA-approved; information is derived from regional (India) prescribing sources, drug references such as MIMS/Medindia, and the nitroimidazole drug class. No EMA SmPC or BNF monograph is available for this agent.
Marketed in India under brand names such as Satrogyl; typical adult dose is 300 mg twice daily for amoebiasis and 600 mg as a single dose for giardiasis or trichomoniasis
Reported to have a shorter half-life (about 1 hour) and lower incidence of neurological and disulfiram-like reactions than metronidazole, but alcohol avoidance is still advised as a class precaution
Generally avoided in pregnancy and lactation, in line with nitroimidazole class caution
Always treat sexual partners concurrently when used for trichomoniasis
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up.
overdose: Specific overdose data are limited. Excessive or prolonged dosing of nitroimidazoles can produce neurologic effects such as peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, confusion, and seizures. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with monitoring of neurologic status. Seek emergency medical care or contact a poison control center.
